title: RandomizedSet — array + HashMap for O(1) insert/remove/getRandom.
shortTitle: RandomizedSet — array plus HashMap for O(1) insert, remove, getRandom

s1_definition.profdef: A RandomizedSet is a data structure that supports inserting an element, removing an element, and returning a uniformly random element, all in average constant time. It combines a dynamic array that stores the actual elements for O(1) random indexing with a hash map from each element to its index in the array, and the removal trick swaps the element to delete with the last array element so that removal never has to shift the array.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the National Bank of India runs a lucky-draw where every eligible account number must have an exactly equal chance of being picked, and accounts are added and removed from eligibility all day. A clerk keeps the account numbers in a numbered list for fair random picking, and a quick index telling where each number sits. To remove an account fast, the clerk moves the last account number into the removed slot and trims the list, so no gap is left and nothing has to be reshuffled.
s1_definition.oneliner: Store elements in an array for fair random indexing and keep a map from element to index, deleting by swapping with the last element so every operation stays constant time.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A RandomizedSet is a data structure that supports inserting an element, removing an element, and returning a uniformly random element, all in average constant time. It combines a dynamic array that stores the actual elements for O(1) random indexing with a hash map from each element to its index in the array, and the removal trick swaps the element to delete with the last array element so that removal never has to shift the array.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine the National Bank of India runs a lucky-draw where every eligible account number must have an exactly equal chance of being picked, and accounts are added and removed from eligibility all day. A clerk keeps the account numbers in a numbered list for fair random picking, and a quick index telling where each number sits. To remove an account fast, the clerk moves the last account number into the removed slot and trims the list, so no gap is left and nothing has to be reshuffled.

**One line to remember:** Store elements in an array for fair random indexing and keep a map from element to index, deleting by swapping with the last element so every operation stays constant time.

sections.s2_technical:
The challenge is that a plain array gives O(1) random access and O(1) append, but removing an arbitrary element from the middle normally costs linear time because everything after it must shift left. A plain hash set gives O(1) insert and remove but cannot pick a uniformly random element in constant time because its internal layout is not indexable.

The RandomizedSet uses both. The array holds the elements in arbitrary order. The hash map maps each element to its current index in the array. To insert, we check the map; if the element is absent we append it to the array and record its index in the map. To get a random element, we generate a random index into the array and return that element, which is uniformly random because every slot is equally likely.

The clever part is remove. To remove an element, we find its index from the map. We take the last element of the array and move it into the index being vacated, update that moved element's index in the map, then shrink the array by removing the last slot, and finally delete the removed element from the map. Because we never shift the middle, removal is constant time, and the random picking stays fair because the array stays densely packed.

A senior nuance: when the element being removed is already the last element, the swap is a no-op but the code must still handle it without corrupting the map. Another nuance is that returning a random element requires a densely packed array with no holes, which is exactly what the swap-with-last technique preserves.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India runs a fair prize draw among currently eligible savings accounts. Accounts become eligible and lose eligibility continuously as balances cross a threshold, and the draw must pick a genuinely uniform random eligible account at any moment.

This is exactly how RandomizedSet works. Any currently present element is equally likely to be returned.

Problem 2 — Eligibility changes must be instant even with millions of accounts, so neither adding nor removing an account can afford to shift a large array or scan a list.

This is exactly why we pair an array with a map and use the swap-with-last removal, keeping insert, remove, and random pick at average constant time.

The code will have a `RandomizedSet` class backed by an `ArrayList` and a `HashMap`, a `Random` for fair picking, and a runnable demo that adds and removes account numbers and draws a random one with logging.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a sequence of inserts, a random draw, a remove, and another draw.

Step 1: `insert("SAV2001")` finds the map empty of that key, appends SAV2001 at array index 0, and records index 0 in the map, returning true.

Step 2: `insert("CUR3001")` appends at index 1 and records it, returning true. A second `insert("SAV2001")` finds the key already present and returns false without changing anything.

Step 3: `insert("SAV4002")` appends at index 2. The array now holds SAV2001, CUR3001, SAV4002 at indices 0, 1, 2.

Step 4: `getRandom()` picks a random index among 0, 1, 2 and returns that account; each has a one-in-three chance.

Step 5: `remove("CUR3001")` reads its index 1, moves the last element SAV4002 into index 1, updates SAV4002's recorded index to 1, trims the array to length 2, and deletes CUR3001 from the map. The array is now SAV2001, SAV4002, densely packed with no hole, so the next `getRandom()` is fair over two elements.

Final output:

```
2026-10-27 13:05:00 INFO    insert SAV2001 -> true
2026-10-27 13:05:00 INFO    insert CUR3001 -> true
2026-10-27 13:05:00 INFO    insert SAV2001 -> false
2026-10-27 13:05:00 INFO    insert SAV4002 -> true
2026-10-27 13:05:00 INFO    random eligible account -> CUR3001
2026-10-27 13:05:00 INFO    remove CUR3001 -> true
2026-10-27 13:05:00 INFO    remove CUR3001 -> false
2026-10-27 13:05:00 INFO    random eligible account -> SAV4002
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  insert SAV2001/CUR3001/SAV4002
    │ array: [SAV2001, CUR3001, SAV4002]
    │ map: {SAV2001:0, CUR3001:1, SAV4002:2}
    ▼
  getRandom → random index in [0,2] → fair pick
    │
    ▼
  remove CUR3001 (idx 1)
    │ move last SAV4002 → slot 1, update map SAV4002:1
    │ trim array, drop CUR3001 from map
    ▼
  array: [SAV2001, SAV4002]  (dense, no hole)
    │ map: {SAV2001:0, SAV4002:1}
    ▼
  getRandom → fair over 2 elements
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
A RandomizedSet is a structure that supports inserting an element, removing an element, and returning a uniformly random element, all in average constant time. The difficulty is that no single built-in collection gives all three cheaply: an array gives fast random indexing and fast append but slow middle removal, while a hash set gives fast insert and remove but cannot pick a uniformly random element in constant time because it is not indexable.

My solution combines the two. I keep a dynamic array holding the elements in arbitrary order, which lets me pick a uniformly random element by generating a random index, and I keep a hash map from each element to its current index in that array. Insertion appends to the array and records the index in the map. The clever part is removal: I look up the element's index, move the last element of the array into that slot, update the moved element's index in the map, shrink the array by one, and delete the removed element from the map. Because I swap with the last element instead of shifting, removal is constant time and the array stays densely packed.

Keeping the array dense is exactly what makes the random pick fair, because every slot is occupied and equally likely. The edge case I always handle is removing the element that is already last, where the swap is effectively a no-op but the map and array must still be updated consistently so nothing is corrupted.

In my project at National Bank of India, we ran a fair prize draw among currently eligible savings accounts, where eligibility changed continuously as balances crossed a threshold. The RandomizedSet let us add and remove accounts from the eligible pool instantly even with millions of accounts, and because the backing array never developed holes, every draw gave each eligible account an exactly equal chance, which was essential for the fairness guarantees the draw had to meet.
